newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Tugs struggle to free Italian flagship off Albania.
newsitem.headline: Tugs struggle to free Italian flagship off Albania.

text.p: The Italian navy cruiser Vittorio Veneto drifted onto a sand bank off the rebel-held port of Vlore on Tuesday while serving as command centre for a multinational security force in Albania. Four tug boats struggled in stormy seas to pull it free.
"Military tugs are trying to get the Vittorio Veneto out of the sand," a spokesman for the Italian defence general staff told Reuters.

The Vittorio Veneto, a cruiser and helicopter carrier, is the flagship of the Italian-led force, which aims to protect aid deliveries to the poor after an armed insurrection triggered by failed investment schemes. Some 160 Italian troops disembarked from Italian navy ships off Vlore on Monday.
Asked when the tugs would free the ship, the spokesman said: "I don't know. It depends on the weather."
Strong winds and rain whipped Vlore as the Vittorio Veneto lay 500 metres (yards) from the shore late on Tuesday, listing slightly to port.
Four tugs tried to pull it from the sand. Two helicopters flew overhead, three small Italian naval boats circled nearby and divers in dinghies criss-crossed the water around the ship.

The Italian navy said in a statement in Rome: "The Vittorio Veneto drifted during buffeting from a strong sirocco wind because the anchor did not hold, and the stern came to rest on the sandy and muddy sea bottom. There is no visible damage to ship or people."
It added that the Vittorio Veneto was still carrying out its command and control duties.
On Vlore beach, a local fisherman said: "I can't believe this boat has got stuck. They had a minesweeper here for three days checking out the area. It can't have done a good job."
He added: "Everyone knows this is not a good place to bring big boats."

Vlore is controlled by a rebel committee, which rejects the authority of President Sali Berisha whom it blames for the collapse of fraudulent investment plans in which many Albanians had invested their life savings. At least 300 people have been killed in the violence in Albania.

In central Albania, 10 battered trucks carrying humanitarian aid from the United Nations World Food Programme reached the worn-down industrial town of Elbasan after a smooth four-hour journey from the port of Durres.

Italian troops secured the roads for the delivery of 220 tonnes of wheat flour. It was the first time that forces from the multinational security mission in Albania had played a role in the distribution of the humanitarian aid.
"There is no malnutrition or starvation but we would like to move fast to prevent that from happening," said WFP spokeswoman Laura Boldrini.
The food was destined for poor families in Elbasan. About 4,430 families living below the poverty line would each be given 50-kg sacks of flour.
"It would not end my worries, but at least I would not have to worry about bread for some time," said a woman named Fatime.

The International Committee of the Red Cross dispatched two deliveries carrying about three tonnes of medicines and food to several locations in northern and south-eastern Albania on Tuesday morning, a spokeswoman said.
The Red Cross, which does not use military escorts, has distributed about 57 tonnes of food and 18 tonnes of medicine since mid-March.
Italy said it had reached an agreement with Albania to help it rebuild its health service.
Italian Health Minister Rosy Bindi signed a deal with her Albanian counterpart Astrit Kalenja after talks in Rome.
"The programme is not just to take care of emergencies but to launch a real reconstruction plan for the Albanian health service," Bindi said.
